reason: The sources provide 18 dual-sourced claims including its daylight visibility, the unique media blackout reason, and the specific fragmentation into four pieces.
story: In 1976, one of the most spectacular visitors in cosmic history arrived—and the world almost missed it. Discovered by Richard West at the European Southern Observatory, Comet West was a 'Great Comet' that reached a staggering magnitude of -3, making it visible in broad daylight. Despite its brilliance, it was largely ignored by the popular media. Burned by the overhyped failure of Comet Kohoutek just three years earlier, scientists and reporters were 'comet-shy.' As the icy wanderer rounded the Sun, the intense gravitational and thermal stress tore its nucleus into four distinct fragments. This traumatic breakup fueled a massive surge in dust, creating a spectral, fan-like tail that stretched 30 degrees across the pre-dawn sky. A survivor from the distant Oort Cloud, Comet West hadn't been seen for 250,000 years. After shattering in the Sun's heat, its pieces drifted back into the abyss, leaving behind one of the greatest displays in astronomical history.
angle: Comet West was so bright it was visible in broad daylight, yet the media ignored it because they were still embarrassed by a previous comet 'dud.'

claims.claim: Comet West was discovered by astronomer Richard M. West.
The comet was discovered using photographs taken on August 10, 1975.
The comet reached its closest approach to the Sun (perihelion) on February 25, 1976.
At its closest, the comet was approximately 0.197 AU from the Sun.
The comet reached a peak apparent magnitude of -3.
Comet West was bright enough to be seen and studied in full daylight.
The comet's nucleus split into four distinct fragments.
Media reporting was minimal because of the disappointing display of Comet Kohoutek in 1973.
The fragments were designated with the letters A, B, C, and D.
The comet's dust tail reached a length of 25 to 30 degrees in the sky.
Forward scattering of sunlight by dust particles significantly enhanced the comet's brightness.
The comet is a long-period wanderer from the Oort Cloud.
The tail featured visible 'synchronic bands' or striations.
Steven O'Meara was the first to observe the comet in daylight using a 9-inch refractor.
The comet's closest approach to Earth occurred on February 29, 1976, at a distance of 0.79 AU.
The comet was last detected in September 1976.
Fragment A was the primary and brightest fragment.
Comet West is officially classified as a 'Great Comet.'

disputed: The exact orbital period is disputed, with estimates ranging from 254,000 years to 558,000 years; the script should refer to it as 'hundreds of thousands of years' (S1, S3, S5, S7).
The exact start date of the nucleus fragmentation is unclear, with one source suggesting a split as early as Feb 19, while others cite March 5 (S1, S5, S6).
